    ONE-AND-A-HALFTH-ORDER LOGIC

    MURDOCH J. GABBAY AND AAD MATHIJSSEN

    Abstract. The practice of ﬁrst-order logic is replete with meta-level concepts. Most notably there are meta-variables ranging over formulae, variables, and terms, and properties of syntax such as alpha-equivalence, capture-avoiding substitution and assumptions about freshness of variables with respect to meta-variables. We present one-and-a-halfth-order logic, in which these concepts are made explicit. We exhibit both sequent and algebraic speciﬁcations of one-and-a-halfth-order logic derivability, show them equivalent, show that the derivations satisfy cut-elimination, and prove correctness of an interpretation of ﬁrst-order logic within it.

    We discuss the technicalities in a wider context as a case-study for nominal algebra, as a logic in its own right, as an algebraisation of logic, as an example of how other systems might be treated, and also as a theoretical foundation for future implementation.

    Aad Mathijsen is supported by the Netherlands Foundation for Scientiﬁc Research (NWO) under grant 612.065.410.

    1. Introduction

    Consider the following valid sequents in ﬁrst-order predicate logic with equality (FOL) [3, 5], written in standard notation:

    (),

    if fn() then ,

    if fn() then (),

    if fn() then ,

    if fn() then ,

    if fn() then () ,

    ().

    These sequents cannot be derived in FOL, since derivations involve FOL syntax only, while the syntax of the sequents just given contains meta-variables , , , and . These are not FOL syntax, they range over it. Also we refer to properties of syntax when we write ‘ fn()’ and ‘’, but FOL syntax cannot represent these explicitly.

    Of course to us humans this is all obvious. One reason is that the derivations fall into a limited number of schema. For example the ‘derivation’ below on the left

    is not a derivation, but it obviously represents a schema of derivations of which the (real) derivation on the right is an instance setting and to . But is there a logic in which the beast on the left is a derivation too?

    It is not a new observation that meta-variables ranging over syntax are not syntax, and that schematic derivations are not derivations [28, page 7] (Hodges calls them ‘argument schema’). Many authors do leave meta-variables at the meta-level. Some suggest that this is where they belong.

    Yet logic teaches us that reasoning can and should be formalised, not only its conclusions. So if we use meta-variables in reasoning, we can and should ask ‘what is the mathematics of this reasoning’?

    This paper presents one-and-a-halfth-order logic. This logic generalises ﬁrst-order logic by adding explicit meta-variables and which in the logic represent the and of the derivations above.

    If we think about how we might do this we immediately encounter serious technical barriers, due to the interaction of meta-variables with quantiﬁers:

    and need not be -convertible if mentions and free. So if we permit predicates with explicit meta-variables such as and , what is the suitable generalisation of -equivalence? It is not acceptable to write ‘ does not occur in the syntax of and ’ (even though this is quite true) — because and are syntax representing unknown predicates and should also represent the intuition of and that they might be instantiated to predicates mentioning .

    Yet we do need to generalise -equivalence, for example so that we can represent the right quantiﬁer introduction rule (R):

    Here as is well-known we expect to be able to -rename to guarantee the side-condition. It is not clear how to do so this in the sequent , for example, because it is not clear how to rename in to avoid capture in .

    In the presence of explicit meta-variables, substitution becomes nontrivial. For example where means ‘replace by ’ has some meaning if we can rely on and being meta-variables which are bound to ‘real’ syntax. What is a correct representation of substitution which permits us to write and thus represent the left introduction rule?

    In this paper we construct a logic which enriches the syntax of ﬁrst-order logic with explicit meta-variables, and which still permits generalised forms of -equivalence, substitution, capture-avoidance, and quantiﬁer introduction rules which are only (a very small distance) away from the ‘schematic derivations’ which we see all the time in informal practice, such as:

    We shall demonstrate not only that such a logic exists, but that it satisﬁes many of the good properties of ﬁrst-order logic including cut-elimination. Even though one-and-a-halfth-order logic is a completely formal logic with clearly-speciﬁed derivation rules, we shall see that reasoning in one-and-a-halfth-order logic is remarkably close to reasoning in informal practice using schematic derivations. One of the obvious future applications of this logic is as a basis for a theorem-prover with some of the generality of second-order logic, but with the ﬂavour of familiar pencil-and-paper schematic derivations in ﬁrst-order logic.

    Map of the paper. In Section 2 we introduce the syntax of one-and-a-halfth-order logic. In Sections 3 to 5 we develop a sequent calculus and establish proof-theoretical properties including cut-elimination. In Section 6 we show that a subset of one-and-a-halfth-order logic is equivalent to ﬁrst-order logic. In Section 7 we give an equational axiomatisation of one-and-a-halfth-order logic and show it equivalent to the sequent calculus. We discuss related and future work in the Conclusions.

    Recall that by our terminology a formula is a term of sort .

    Our rules resemble those of Gentzen’s sequent calculus for classical ﬁrst-order logic with equality [9, 24, 42], but with the following distinctive features:

    Unknown formulae and unknown terms are represented explicitly as unknowns of sort and respectively.

    We can make freshness assumptions about unknowns (using (Fr)), and these aﬀect derivability, for example in (R).

    A theory of equality of terms up to -equivalence and capture-avoiding substitution is represented by an equality ∆ in a theory SUB (formally deﬁned in the next section).

    Side-conditions on substitution, freshness and atoms not occurring in terms, are all decidable.

    (StructL) and (StructR) are so-called structural rules, which help us manage substitutions (see the example derivations in Figure 3). Note that the side-conditions of these rules refer to equational derivability in SUB.

    (Fr) lets us introduce fresh atoms into a derivation. The diﬃculty which this rule addresses is the explicit meta-variables of nominal terms; we need (Fr) to add explicit information that the atom is fresh for them, into the freshness context.

    We have seen examples of one-and-a-halfth-order logic derivations. We have seen that structural rules and freshnesses play an important rôle in the control of the explicit meta-variables.

    5. Proof-theoretical results

    This section shows two important properties of the sequent calculus for one-and-a-halfth order logic:

    In derivations, atoms may be permuted and unknowns may be instantiated. We will call these properties equivariance and substitution.

    The cut-elimination property of ﬁrst-order predicate logic is preserved by the extension to one-and-a-halfth-order logic.

    5.1. Equivariance and substitution.

    Fix a freshness context ∆, a context and cocontext Φ and Ψ, and a derivation Π.

    We extend notation for permutation and substitution actions , and to contexts Φ and cocontexts Ψ, writing Φ, Φ and Φ, and Ψ, Ψ and Ψ for the result of applying the actions to the terms in the syntax of Φ and Ψ.

    Write Π for the derivation obtained from Π by replacing every sequent Φ Ψ by Φ Ψ.

    Theorem 5.1 (Meta-level equivariance).

    Suppose that Π is a valid derivation of Φ Ψ. Then Π is a valid derivation of Φ Ψ.

    Proof

    Recall that Π is a tree labelled with (nominal algebra) syntax, ∆is a set of syntax, and Φ, and Ψ are syntax. These may all mention atoms. Recall also that the notion of ‘valid derivation’ depends on a nominal algebra theory SUB, and that SUB is syntax too (a set of axioms) which mention two atoms and . The statement

    ‘Π is a valid derivation of Φ Ψ’ can be expressed by a ZFA predicate (Appendix A) with parameters ∆, Π, Φ, Ψ, and the axioms in SUB.2

    By ZFA equivariance (Theorem A.3) validity is invariant under permuting atoms in the parameters. By a remarkable coincidence we have characterised this permutation action inductively for the data we care about; this is exactly -. So if the statement above is true, then so is

    ‘Π is a valid derivation of Φ Ψ’, where we use SUB to check side-conditions.

    By Lemma 4.9 derivability in SUB is identical to derivability in SUB. The result follows.

    Some terminology is useful for Theorems 5.2, and 5.3. Suppose Π is a derivation. It may use the rule (Fr), which introduces fresh atoms into the derivation (if we read the derivation bottom-up), or which garbage-collects fresh atoms in the derivation (if we read the derivation top-down). Call these the fresh atoms of Π.3 We will use this notion to phrase accidental name clash conditions in the next theorems.

    Write Π for the derivation obtained from Π by replacing each sequent Φ Ψ by Φ Ψ.

    Theorem 5.2 (Object-level equivariance).

    Suppose that is a permutation and suppose that Π is a valid derivation of Φ Ψ whose fresh atoms are disjoint from the atoms in .

    Then Π is a valid derivation of Φ Ψ.

    Proof

    By induction on Π. Base cases (Ax) and (L) are direct. We consider the inductive cases in turn:

    (1) The case of (R): Suppose Φ Ψ is derived using (R). Then there exists a derivation of Φ Ψ, and by the inductive hypothesis is a derivation of Φ Ψ. Then

    is the required derivation Π of Φ Ψ.

    The cases (L), (L), (L) and (R) are similar.

    (2) The case of (R): Suppose Φ Ψ is derived using (R). Then #Φ Ψ holds and is a derivation of Φ Ψ. By Lemma 4.5 # Φ Ψ, and by inductive hypothesis is a derivation of Φ Ψ. We conclude that Φ Ψ is derivable by extending with (R), as required.

    The cases (StructL), (StructR) and (Cut) are similar.

    (3) The case of (Fr): Suppose Φ Ψ is derived using (Fr). Then there exists a derivation of Φ Ψ where Φ Ψ ∆. By the inductive hypothesis is a derivation of Φ Ψ. By assumption (, so Φ Ψ ∆and we conclude Φ Ψ using (Fr). The assumption on fresh atoms prevents us from an accidental clash that occurs if the introduced atom is present in .

    7. An equational axiomatisation of one-and-a-halfth-order logic

    In Section 3 we introduced (the sequent calculus of) one-and-a-halfth-order logic and in Section 4 we introduced nominal algebra. In this section we give an axiomatic presentation of one-and-a-halfth-order logic in nominal algebra.

    7.1. Theory FOL.

    Definition 7.1

    Let theory FOL be given by the axioms of theory SUB (Figure 5) plus the axioms of Figure 9.

    We now discuss the axioms in Figure 9:

    We read (MP) as ‘Modus Ponens’. Modus Ponens is the principle “if ‘’ is true and ‘ implies ’ is true, then ‘’ is true”. In our algebraic setting the judgement ‘is true’ is rendered as ‘= ’.

    Lemma 7.2

    If we read ‘is true’ as ‘’ then (MP) implies Modus Ponens.

    Proof

    Suppose that and that . Then by the rules for equality. We conclude by (MP).

    In (M) recall that is sugar for . This axiom from [33], along with Modus Ponens, is suﬃcient as a Hilbert-style proof-system [30] to derive the notion of truth of classical propositional logic. Expressed as an algebra as above, the two axioms yield an implication-only version of boolean algebra [7].

    (M) stands for Meredith, the author of this axiom for classical predicate logic, which he discovered in the 1940s. Machine-checked veriﬁcation of this fact is online [34]. Succinct axioms for propositional logic continue to provide innocent fun in some circles [32]; a good survey is here [23].

    Axioms (Q1) (Q3) add quantiﬁers; (Q3) exploits freshness conditions. These axioms appear in the literature [14, page 5 (2)]. What is new here is that our axioms are not axiom-schemes; they are individual axioms (three, to be precise). We do this using the unknowns of nominal terms, and abstractions and freshness conditions to express capture-avoidance conditions which usually must be expressed — at the meta-level — for every instance. Note how these axioms are faithful to the usual syntactic form of the axiom-schemes found in the literature.

    Axioms (E1) and (E2) add object-level equality.

    Again, we are able to represent by two axioms what might otherwise be two inﬁnite axiom-schemes.

    is non-empty because it is populated by atoms (in the derivation above, we use the fact that it is populated by ). Thanks to the substitution action, atoms behave like ‘object-level variable symbols’. Normally sorts of terms are populated by variable symbols, but this feature of the syntax does not show in the semantics, and that aﬀects the notion of derivability: () may be derivable. We see that in one-and-a-halfth-order logic terms are populated by unknowns and atoms. Although atoms represent variable symbols, the derivation above suggests that any semantics for one-and-a-halfth-order logic must diﬀer from a ‘standard’ semantics, and give atoms denotational reality. One such semantics is given by a standard semantics for nominal algebra [21] in nominal sets [22]; developing other denotations-containing-variables is very much of current research interest.

    8. Conclusions

    One-and-a-halfth-order logic generalises ﬁrst-order logic by internalising meta-level variables that range over syntax. Thanks to the use of nominal techniques, the sequent rules from Figure 2 accurately reﬂect common practice in the handling of these meta-variables (compare for instance the examples in the Introduction to the formal derivations in Figure 3). We have been able to import ﬁrst-order logic proof theory quite directly into our augmented setting, and also given an algebraic axiomatisation using Nominal Algebra.

    The technical tools used in this paper were developed based on work on Nominal Uniﬁcation by the ﬁrst author with Urban and Pitts [45], which introduced the theory of nominal terms up to CORE (our terminology). This was extended with Fernández [13] to Nominal Rewriting, a theory of rewriting on nominal terms, again up to CORE, and recently investigated with the second author, as a general framework of nominal algebra [21, 18].

    8.1. Related work.

    We discuss the relation of the work in this paper to ﬁrst-order logic with binders, second-order and higher-order logics, and algebraic logic.

    First-order logic with binders. Typically Gentzen’s sequent calculus is taken to have a ﬁrst-order term-language. Logics exist in the style of ﬁrst-order logic, but whose terms include binding. One of them is binding logic of Dowek et. al. [10], which was intended as a general-purpose ﬁrst-order logic for studying term-languages with binding. Another one is Beeson’s lambda-logic [4], which was intended for the speciﬁc application of manipulating lambda-terms, in a ﬁrst-order logic.

    The term-language of one-and-a-halfth-order logic natively supports binders: the sorting arities of the object-level term-formers and predicate term-formers allow for abstractions [] and [] as their arguments. Therefore the results on Genzten’s sequent calculus we have stated in Section 6 can, we think, be extended naturally to many of the ‘ﬁrst-order ﬂavoured’ logics with term-formers enriched with binders; the machinery is already there.

    Note that one-and-a-halfth-order logic is diﬀerent from lambda-logic and binding logic. For example the syntax used in this paper includes explicit meta-variables.

    Second-order and higher-order logics. Monadic second-order logic enriches ﬁrst-order logic with variables ranging over sets of elements [8]; these can be identiﬁed with function variables of type where is a type of individuals and a type of truth-values (for example and respectively). Second-order enriches ﬁrst-order logic with variables ranging over -ary relations; these can be identiﬁed with function variables of type . Higher-order logic enriches ﬁrst-order logic with variables ranging over a full type-hierarchy, inductively deﬁnable by [46, 43, 12]. Such function variables can be used to represent meta-variables. However, this representation inherits some very particular features from its intended functional semantics:

    You have to choose the arity of your meta-variable in advance. A meta-variable can be interpreted as a function variable

    — but for which ? The representation distributes meta-variables across many types.

    Perhaps more importantly, instantiation of these function variables avoids capture. This has a side-eﬀect that it is not possible to represent a meta-variable uniformly across contexts. For example to represent a meta-variable in the context we can intuitively express as , it suﬃces to write where : ; but to represent in the context we must write — must take a higher type. Since for any given we must choose a type for it, it is not possible to directly represent the context we might write as Qs, where Qs represents an unknown context (of quantiﬁers).

    Instantation of unknowns in nominal algebra does not avoid capture so that accurately reﬂects our intention when we write where may be instantiated in a capturing manner. Furthermore still represents in .

    Moving to higher orders engenders certain computational diﬃculties [31]. For example uniﬁcation up to -equivalence is not decidable (restrictions of it are in [36]), while uniﬁcation up to CORE is decidable [45].

    Still, quotienting terms by is convenient, as exploited by theorem-provers such as Isabelle [38, 39] and Coq [29]. It remains to be seen whether nominal algebra or something like it can enjoy the success and usefulness enjoyed by these systems.

    A direct comparison between one-and-a-halfth-order logic and second-order logic is not possible. The second-order theorem (() ) cannot be expressed in one-and-a-halfth-order logic, because one-and-a-halfth-order logic has no quantiﬁcation over predicates; this gives it a ﬁrst-order ﬂavour. On the other hand the one-and-a-halfth-order logic theorem cannot be expressed in second-order logic, because that logic cannot directly express freshness conditions. The authors are not aware of any truly satisfactory account of the precise relation of nominal-style unknowns and higher-order variables.

    Algebraic logic. Our work is one (more) element in a very long line of investigations into algebraic logic [1]; for example cylindric [27], polyadic [26], and quantiﬁer [41] algebra. There too, unknowns are syntax representing unknown elements quantiﬁed universally at top level, and abstraction []- (our notation) is clearly visible, e.g. as the of cylindric algebra. However, these systems do not have as a goal to reﬂect the proof-theory of ﬁrst-order logic. One-and-a-halfth-order logic does this. The connection with the algebraic method is then via Nominal Algebra and our axiomatisation of derivability in one-and-a-halfth-order logic.

    Deep and shallow embeddings. We can represent the syntax of ﬁrst-order logic in a so-called framework logical system, at ‘object-level’, i.e. as an inductive datatype — the so-called deep embedding. Then meta-variables are easily representable as meta-variables of the framework. This path is taken by Higher-Order Abstract Syntax [40], Fraenkel-Mostowski syntax [22], the Theory of Contexts [35] and much other research. This enterprise is quite diﬀerent from that undertaken in this paper; one-and-a-halfth-order logic is about extending the syntax of the logic itself so it contains something which behaves very much like a meta-variable ranging over unknown formulae, without losing logical properties such as cut-elimination.

    It is also possible to represent the semantics of ﬁrst-order logic as a theory in a framework, for example as a pair of types and along with functions between them like : or : () . This is called a shallow embedding.

    In [39] the case is made for Isabelle and for its higher-order logic framework as an eﬃcient basis for shallow embeddings, and for conducting mathematics in these embeddings. For example, a shallow embedding of ﬁrst-order logic called Isabelle/FOL exists in Isabelle’s higher-order logic framework Isabelle/Pure. Our axiomatisation of one-and-a-halfth-order logic in nominal algebra is a shallow embedding.

    The technical content of this paper is therefore in two halves with equal status: a case study of a shallow embedding of ﬁrst-order logic using nominal algebra as a logical framework, and a study of logic proof-theory in the presence of nominal-style unknowns.

    8.2. Future work.

    We believe that there is no technical barrier to creating a variant of one-and-a-halfth-order logic that corresponds to intuitionistic logic [47] with meta-variables; it can be deﬁned in the usual way by restricting the sequents in Figure 2 to have a single conclusion. Also developing a formal semantics should not pose many problems: evaluate unknowns to terms and then evaluate atoms to elements of a set underlying domain.

    The following describes some more challenging future work.

    Incomplete proofs. We have internalised meta-variables that range over terms and formulae. We can also consider meta-variables ranging over incomplete proofs. Incomplete proofs arise naturally in proof-search in a human-assisted theorem-prover such as Isabelle or Coq. Here the theorem-prover acts as a program to manipulate proofs which are incomplete both in the sense of having holes, and in the sense of occurring in an unknown context, and the human assistant guides the system to ﬁll in these holes until a complete proof emerges. A quantiﬁer introduction rule binds the quantiﬁed variable in the derivation above it (this is usually expressed by a freshness condition). In the presence of incomplete proofs it is necessary to somehow represent this binding over an as yet unknown derivation.

    We believe that nominal terms with their unknowns and abstractions are a good match for the incomplete proofs and quantiﬁers binding in it. As the incomplete proof is ‘ﬁlled in’ by the human assistant and the system, a capturing substitution should be made for the unknown. An exciting application of our technology would be an investigation of how well (if at all) a system related to one-and-a-halfth-order logic but with proof-terms can represent this process. This would also provide us with a basis for the implementation of a theorem-prover with some of the generality of second-order logic, but with the ﬂavour of familiar pencil-and-paper schematic derivations in ﬁrst-order logic.

    Hierarchies of variables. We see one-and-a-halfth-order logic as the ﬁrst of a family of two-level logics as yet to be created. For example we would like to be able to quantify over unknowns anywhere in a formula, which allows us to write an expressions like

    This is current research.

    We are also interested in logics with inﬁnite hierarchies of stronger meta-variables such that at each level a meta-variable of higher level behaves to the lower level as an unknown behaves to an atom . This idea is explored in the arena of operational semantics by a -calculus called the lambda-context calculus [17], and a rewriting framework called hierarchical nominal rewriting [16]. This might recover some or all of the power which one-and-a-halfth-order logic lacks compared to higher-order logic, but in a diﬀerent way. In short, we envisage two- three- four- and -and-a-halfth-order logic. This would involve interesting extensions to the ‘nominal theme’.

    Axiomatisation of substructural logics. Based on our experience with the axiomatisation of ﬁrst-order logic in Section 7, we see no diﬃculties in principle with axiomatising substructural logics such as linear logic [25], bunched implications [37], relevance logics [11], and so on; if the logic is susceptible to a (nominal) algebraic treatment then it can be axiomatised in nominal algebra. This is not always the case of a shallow embedding in a higher-order logical framework, because the structural rules of the connectives and quantiﬁers of the framework may ‘infect’ those of the object-logic.

    Nominal foundations of mathematics. Higher-order logic models quantiﬁers as elements of () . Many logical frameworks are based on this, for example Isabelle/FOL and Isabelle/HOL. Proofs of basic properties such as Church-Rosser, in Isabelle or systems like it, rest on the correctness of higher-order logic and so depend amongst other things on Church-Rosser. One-and-a-halfth order logic and nominal algebra suggest the tantalising prospect that a new and arguably elementary foundation for mathematics and logical frameworks might be created, one which could be a close match for the ‘mathematics of the informal meta-level’ which we see used daily in informal mathematical discourse.

    Appendix A. Equivariance

    We use atoms in this paper — we introduce them when we write ‘Fix a countably inﬁnite collection of atoms ’ in Section 2.

    We can represent atoms as, say, numbers 0 1 2 3, or as sets . In principle we might ‘accidentally’ use some property of atoms speciﬁc to their implementation, such as or . However, we know we do not do this, because we consider atoms to be atomic.

    By explicitly bearing this in mind, we can rename atoms. This is equivariance, proved below, which we use freely in this paper to give structural inductive proofs (renaming atoms in inductive hypotheses where convenient) while remaining fully formal.

    If we wish to be fully formal but ignore equivariance we must work by induction on measures such as term length or derivation depth. These are longer, harder to read, and are rarely given in full detail outside of a theorem-prover.

    To give a precise statement and formal proof of equivariance and how it can be used to rename atoms in proofs by structural induction on the syntax of terms and derivation-trees we use a foundational theory: Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory with atoms (ZFA). ZFA has equivariance [6] and because it is known that set theory can be used to formalise mathematics, equivariance is a meta-mathematical property which we can use in the proofs in this paper.5

    We do not mean that equivariance refers to the terms of sort , nor the formulae of ﬁrst-order logic, nor sequents of one-and-a-halfth-order logic. We mean that it refers to the assertions written in english in this paper — about one-and-a-halfth-order logic, nominal algebra, and so on.

    ZFA features a set of atoms . The original motivation of atoms was to address the question ‘what set is equal to Plato?’. Obviously Plato is not any of the ‘normal’ sets of set theory, such as the empty set or the set containing just the empty set , and so on. The answer was to accommodate ‘the real world’ by introducing it en masse into the set model, as atoms.

    As far as the set theory is concerned atoms are atomic objects with no internal (set-)structure, so it is quite natural to use these to model variable symbols. This idea appears already in [2].

    For the language of ZFA set theory, in addition to the basic language of ﬁrst-order logic with equality, we assume:

    A binary predicate symbol called set inclusion.

    A constant term-former called the set of atoms.

    We use standard sugar of classical logic (similar to the sugar mentioned in Subsection 2.1).
